rv.q: Ms. Peters gives a performance of stupendous technical accomplishment, one that captures not merely the mannerisms but the essence of Judy Garland's tragic persona.
But all of this comic shtick starts to wear thin pretty quickly, and the playwright's efforts to inject drama into the proceedings are even less successful.
Ms. Harper camps and vamps with determined proficiency, injecting plenty of life if not much verisimilitude into Mr. Lombardo’s cruel but enjoyably catty cliché.

With the corners of her mouth dragged down to her ankles, a cigarette in one hand and a drink in the other, Ms. Harper camps and vamps with determined proficiency, injecting plenty of life if not much verisimilitude into Mr. Lombardo’s cruel but enjoyably catty cliché.

But if wisecracks are the highlight, you might as well put on a one-woman musical—as Tovah Feldshuh and Helen Gallagher have done—instead of a play, which requires sound structure and character development.
But because that focus so often strays from where it seems it should belong, what should be a completely rollicking evening is frequently a rough and rumpled one.

cn.t: Harper's performance as Tallulah Bankhead earns praise, but critics find Lombardo's play thinly stretches a single anecdote into two hours, resulting in a one-note biographical sketch that wears thin despite occasional comic moments.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
